Destroyer Monaghan, 28 Apr 1938

The USS Monaghan (DD 354) was a Farragut-class destroyer that had one of the most eventful and ultimately tragic careers of any American destroyer in World War II.

She was commissioned in April 1935 and named after Ensign John R. Monaghan, a U.S. Navy officer killed in Samoa in 1899. By the time war came to the Pacific, she was based at Pearl Harbor as part of Destroyer Division 2.

Monaghan was the ready-duty destroyer that morning, meaning she was the one ship kept on short notice to get underway. As the Japanese air attack unfolded, she was ordered to assist USS Ward, which had reported attacking a submarine outside the harbor entrance. While steaming out, Monaghan spotted a Japanese Type A midget submarine inside the harbor itself. She opened fire, then rammed the submarine and dropped depth charges, sinking it. The collision damaged her stern but she stayed in the fight. This made her one of the first U.S. ships to score a confirmed kill in the war.

In May 1942 she screened the carrier task forces at the Battle of the Coral Sea, the first carrier-versus-carrier engagement in history. A month later she was part of the screen for USS Enterprise at the Battle of Midway, helping protect the carriers during the decisive American victory that broke the back of Japanese naval air power.

Monaghan was sent north to the cold and brutal Aleutian campaign. On March 26, 1943, she fought in the Battle of the Komandorski Islands, an unusual daylight surface gun duel between American and Japanese cruiser-destroyer forces. It was one of the longest continuous gunnery actions of the war, fought without air support on either side, and it ended with the Japanese breaking off and abandoning their attempt to resupply the garrison on Attu. Monaghan later supported the landings at Attu and Kiska.

She moved south to the Central Pacific drive, screening fast carrier groups and supporting amphibious operations at Tarawa, Kwajalein, Eniwetok, the Marianas (including the Battle of the Philippine Sea), and the early Leyte operations. By late 1944 she had earned 12 battle stars.

Her end came not in combat but in weather. While Admiral William Halsey's Third Fleet was attempting to refuel east of the Philippines, it was caught by Typhoon Cobra, a violent storm Halsey had badly underestimated. Monaghan, like several other destroyers, was running low on fuel, which meant her ballast was light and she rode high and unstable. As the seas built to roughly 70-foot waves with winds well over 100 knots, she lost steering, rolled heavily, and finally capsized.

Out of a crew of about 256, only 6 men survived, picked up from a raft three days later. Two sister destroyers, USS Hull and USS Spence, went down in the same storm. Nearly 800 sailors were lost across the three ships, making it one of the worst non-combat disasters in U.S. Navy history.

A court of inquiry found that command failures and inadequate weather information had contributed to the disaster. The investigation led to lasting changes: better fleet weather forecasting, the establishment of dedicated typhoon warning centers in the Pacific, stricter rules on ballasting low-fuel destroyers, and revised stability criteria for top-heavy ship designs. The lessons from Monaghan, Hull, and Spence shaped U.S. Navy practice for decades afterward.
